report_unavailable_tool:image — The image-generation tool is unavailable, so I can’t create a bitmap. Below is a concise, ready-to-follow plan so you (or an artist) can paint a square watercolor illustration of a lighthouse in fog.

Materials (compact)
- Watercolor paper, 300 gsm, square (suggest 25 × 25 cm / 10 × 10 in)
- Brushes: large mop/wash (1"), round #6, round #2 or rigger, flat or filbert for edges
- Palette, water jars, paper towel, masking fluid (optional), sponge/tissue
- Pigments: Ultramarine Blue, Payne’s Gray (or Neutral Tint), Burnt Sienna, Yellow (Hansa or Cadmium Light), Alizarin Crimson or Quinacridone Rose

Composition (quick)
- Square format. Place lighthouse slightly off-center (about 1/3 from right), horizon low (lower 1/4) so fog/sky dominates. Keep negative space above for fog.

Color recipe (mix hints)
- Fog wash: very dilute Payne’s Gray + a touch Ultramarine (approx 1:20 paint:water)
- Tower neutral base: Ultramarine 2 : Burnt Sienna 1 (muted cool gray)
- Dark accents: add a little Payne’s Gray to the base mix
- Lantern glow: pale Yellow + tiny Alizarin (very dilute) for warm glow

Step-by-step painting (concise)

1) Light sketch
- Pencil-sketched lighthouse silhouette and faint horizon. Keep lines minimal.

2) Optional masking
- Mask the lantern window(s) and any bright highlights you want completely white.

3) Wet-on-wet background (foggy sky)
- Wet the entire paper lightly with clean water.
- Drop in the very dilute fog wash from top working downward; let pigment feather and dilute more toward the horizon so the lower area stays palest.
- Tilt or blot with tissue to encourage soft vertical streaks. Keep edges feathered and soft.

4) Define distant sea/horizon
- While background is damp-to-dry, add a slightly cooler, slightly darker horizontal band near the horizon with diluted Ultramarine + Payne’s Gray to suggest distant water—soft edges.

5) Paint the lighthouse base (after background dries to touch)
- Use wet-on-dry for sharper silhouette. Block in the lighthouse with the neutral base mix. Keep forms simple: tower, lantern room, small balcony.
- Soften the top edges into the fog by lightly lifting with a damp clean brush or tissue while paint is still slightly damp to blend.

6) Add mid and dark values
- Add darker stripes, railing, door, and shadow side with a stronger wash (more pigment). Use a rigger or round #2 for thin rail lines.
- Keep contrast low–the fog mutes values; avoid pure black.

7) Lantern glow
- Remove masking if used. Lay a very soft, warm glaze around the lantern: dilute Yellow (tiny Alizarin if desired) in a circular halo. Soften edges by feathering outward with a damp brush to suggest light diffused by fog.
- Leave the center bright (lift with tissue if needed).

8) Foreground rocks/waves (minimal)
- Indicate a few low-value rocks or a dark, softened silhouette at the base using drybrush strokes and lifted highlights. Keep them subdued so fog remains dominant.

9) Texture and atmosphere
- Use lifting (clean damp brush or tissue) to create streaks or mist patches. Sprinkle a little table salt on semi-dry areas for subtle grain (optional). Use a toothbrush splatter lightly for distant spray—do this sparingly.

10) Final adjustments
- Add a few thin dark accents (door, railing) for focal definition. Check overall values: reduce contrast if too crisp by glazing a very dilute fog wash over the whole piece to unify.
- Let dry fully, then remove masking fluid and refine any tiny highlights.

Timing notes
- Work from light to dark; allow background to dry where you need sharp edges. Use lifting and glazes to control softness.

This plan will produce a square watercolor of a lighthouse shrouded in fog with soft atmospherics and a warm lantern glow.
